newsitem.title: peru: Talks to resume in Peru crisis, reporters freed.
newsitem.headline: Talks to resume in Peru crisis, reporters freed.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis began a more hopeful phase on Saturday as the government and rebels prepared to end nearly two weeks of stalemate in talks and two Japanese TV employees arrested after interviewing the hostage-takers were released from jail.

The Peruvian antiterrorist police DINCOTE released two employees of Japanese television station TV Asahi who were arrestedon Tuesday after meeting Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages in the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador in Lima, a TV Asahi official said.
"They have been released," the official told a news conference, referring to TV Asahi reporter Tsuyoshi Hitomi and his Peruvian interpreter Victor Borja.
Hitomi would leave Peru later on Saturday on a flight to New York, where he is based, the official said.
The Peruvian and Japanese governments had criticised the two men for sneaking into the residence to meet the rebels, saying they had jeopardised efforts to end the 25-day-old stand-off.

After nearly two weeks of stalled negotiations, government negotiator Domingo Palermo spoke on Friday with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini by radio to arrange a face-to-face meeting this weekend.
Although the meeting did not take place on Saturday, Roman Catholic bishop Juan Carlos Cipriani entered the residence to visit the hostages.
"We hope these contacts will achieve developments which will lead to a peaceful resolution to the crisis," an official for the Japanese government's task force in Lima said.
"I am optimistic that everything will turn out well," Cipriani told reporters before entering the residence.

The MRTA initially took more than 500 hostages when it stormed a cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17, but has released most since then. It is holding the most valuable hostages as bargaining chips to obtain its principal demand: the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
Palermo, whose first face-to-face meeting with Cerpa on Dec. 28 brought the release of 20 hostages, had not entered the residence by late Saturday afternoon.
Red Cross officials continued to shuttle to and fro, taking in food and supplies. For the first time, books in Japanese were delivered for the Japanese captives.
The only sign of life from the roughly 15 MRTA members inside was the brief appearance at a window of one young rebel dressed in black who watched photographers on a nearby rooftop with binoculars.
When asked by the photographers how the hostages were, the rebel first replied "screwed up" and then "fine."

Asked if there would be more hostage releases or if the rebels were still demanding from the government the freedom of all their jailed comrades, he waved his hands in a gesture interpreted by some journalists as meaning "No."

Outside the residence, police detained another suspected MRTA member posing as a journalist, local radio reported. Oscar Chumpitaz was apprehended carrying false documents, a camera and binoculars, Radio Programas said.
DINCOTE, who could not immediately confirm the information, have previously arrested about six MRTA suspects seeking to liaise with their comrades inside the besieged residence.
Saturday's activity followed a week of heightened rhetoric between the government and the Marxist MRTA. Although both sides agreed to talk again, neither has made any concessions.

Fujimori has insisted he will not give in to "terrorist blackmail" and urged the rebels to lay down their arms and release all the captives. But the MRTA has reiterated it will not leave the residence until it obtains the release of some 400 jailed comrades.
The government has, however, floated the possibility of granting the rebels political exile abroad if they surrender.
Palermo insisted the government would accept nothing short of the release of all the remaining captives.

Red Cross spokesman Steven Anderson said on Saturday that, as well as attending to the hostages' needs, the organisation "served as a channel at the disposition of the government and the MRTA to facilitate a solution to the crisis."

The daily La Republica reported on Saturday that Peru's secret military court had convicted an MRTA member for his involvement in the 1995 kidnapping of a former Bolivian planning minister. That kidnapping raised some of the money used for the MRTA's current hostage-taking operation in Lima.

Roque Gonzales La Rosa was sentenced on Dec. 12 to 20 years in a maximum security jail for his role in the Nov. 1995 abduction of Samuel Doria Medina in the Bolivian capital by nine MRTA members, the newspaper said.
